overview.body:
**Bhakti** (*bhakti*) ​— Devotion, ‌Loving Attachment ‌to the ​Divine · ​Devotion, loving ​attachment, faith ​— worship ​and piety ‌directed toward the ​divine, esp ​— belongs ‌to the ​Sanskrit tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Devotion, ​Love". The name ​means "Devotion, ​loving attachment, ​faith — ‌worship and ​piety directed ‌toward the ​divine, esp. ‌as a religious ​principle and ‌means of ​salvation."[^1].

**Bhakti** ‌is devotion ​as a ​complete path: ‌the loving ‌attachment to ‌a personal god ​that the ​Bhagavadgītā crowns ‌as the ​easiest and ​swiftest way, ‌and that ​the medieval ​saints of ‌Tamil country made ​into India’s ‌most popular ​religion. From ​temple hymns ​sung in ​the vernacular ‌to the ‌quiet love ​of the quietist ‌traditions, bhakti ​is the ​subcontinent’s answer ‌to the ‌question: how ‌shall an ‌ordinary person ​love the ‌infinite?[^2]

PuniCodex restores ​the name ​as **Bhakti** ​and serves ‌its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/bhakti/). The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ‌form — a ​description computed ​from the ​displayed form ‌itself. The ​plain ASCII ‌form *bhakti* ​survives as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed by ‌the early ‌domain-name system; ​the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Devanagari as ​**भक्ति**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"Devotion, ‌loving attachment, ​faith ​— ‌worship and ​piety ‌directed ​toward the ‌divine, ​esp. as ​a ​religious ​principle and ​means ‌of ​salvation."[^1].

The ‌ASCII ​form *bhakti* ‌survives ​only ‌because the ​early ‌domain-name ​system could ​not ‌carry diacritics; ‌it ‌is ​a technological ​compromise, ‌not ​an ancient ​spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration ​**Bhakti** ‌recovers the ​full ‌diacritic ​detail of ​the ​scholarly transliteration ​directly ‌in ‌the address ​bar. ‌The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ‌— a ‌description ‌computed ‌from the ​displayed ‌form ​itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

- ‌**b** ​→ ​**B** — ​Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**h** → ​**h** ​— Same
- ‌**a** ​→ ‌**a** — ​Same
- ‌**k** ​→ **k** ‌— ‌Same
- **t** ​→ ​**t** ​— Same
- ​**i** ‌→ ‌**i** — ​Same

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is ​**/ˈbʌkti/** — ​Sanskrit ​(IAST: ‌Bhakti).[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ‌**Bh-** ​— ‌The bh ​is ‌a ​voiced ​aspirate — ​“b” ​with ​breath; ‌not a ​plain ‌English ​b.
- ‌**-ak-** — ​Short ‌a ​as ‌in “cup”; ​the ​root ‌is ‌bhaj, “to ‌share, ​partake, ​adore”.
- ‌**-ti** — ​The ​abstract ‌ending: ​“devotion”, “participation” ​— ‌the ​quality ‌made a ​noun.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ‌the ‌closest ​approximation ‌is: “BUK-tee”

​Kindred ​and ‌historical ‌forms of ‌the ‌name:

- ​**Root** ‌— √bhaj ​— ​to ​share, ‌to serve, ​to ​worship
- ​**Tamil** ‌— paripāṭu/paṭi ​— ​the ​Tamil ‌bhakti of ​the ‌Āḻvārs

​The ‌word begins ​as ‌“partaking” ‌— ​devotion as ​sharing ​in ​the ‌divine, not ‌mere ​adoration.

domains.body:
**Bhakti** ​is devotion ‌as ‌a complete ​path: the ​loving ​attachment to ​a ​personal god ‌that ​the Bhagavadgītā ​crowns ‌as the ​easiest and ‌swiftest ​way, and ‌that ​the medieval ​saints ​of Tamil ​country ​made into ‌India’s most ​popular ‌religion. From ​temple ‌hymns sung ​in ‌the vernacular ​to ‌the quiet ​love of ​the ‌quietist traditions, ‌bhakti ‌is the ​subcontinent’s ​answer to ‌the ​question: how ​shall an ‌ordinary ​person love ​the ‌infinite?[^1]

### The ​Path ‌of Love

​The ​Bhagavadgītā’s ninth ​teaching: “offer ​me ‌even a ‌leaf, ​a flower, ‌a ​fruit, water ​— ‌I accept ‌it”.

### The ‌Āḻvārs

‌The twelve ​Tamil ‌poet-saints whose ​hymns ​to Viṣṇu ​founded ‌the tradition ​— composed, ​not ​compiled.

### Nāma-Saṅkīrtana

‌The ​chanting of ​the ​name — ‌Hare ​Krishna, Rāma ‌Rāma — ​as ‌devotion’s simplest ​engine.

### ‌Grace over ‌Works

​Prapatti, śaraṇāgati ​— ​the “surrender” ​that asks ‌nothing ‌and receives ​everything.

mythology.body:
Bhakti has ​no biography — ‌it is the ‌biography of millions. ​Its ‘myths’ are ​the movement’s own ​history: the Gītā’s ​canonization of devotion, ​the Tamil saints’ ‌songs, the Maharashtrian ​kīrtan, and the ​global chant of ‌the Hare Krishna ​movement. The tradition’s ‌foundational stories cluster ​around the saints ‌themselves — the ​hagiographies of Mirabai, ​Tukaram, and the ​gopīs of Braj.[^1]

### ​The Easiest Path ​(Bhagavadgītā 9)

Krishna’s ‌ninth discourse tells the ​anxious that devotion ‌needs no learning, ​no wealth, no ‌austerity: a leaf, ​a flower, a ‌fruit, water — ​given with love, ‌accepted. The verse ​is the charter ​of every subsequent ‌bhakti movement, and ‌the most quoted ‌single sentence of ​the Gītā in ​the modern world.[^2]

### ‌The Poet-Saints of ​Tamil Country (Āḻvār ​Cycle)

Between the ‌sixth and ninth ​centuries, twelve poet-saints ​— Nammāḻvār foremost ‌— sang Viṣṇu ​into Tamil verse, ‌walking the temple ​towns and composing ​the Nālāyira Divya ​Prabandham, four thousand ​hymns still sung ‌daily. The bhakti ‌they invented was ​personal, vernacular, and ‌ecstatic — religion ​in the mother-tongue, ​against the Sanskrit ‌monopoly.

### The Love ‌of the Gopīs ‌(Gopī Cycle)

The ‌Bhāgavata Purāṇa’s tenth ​book tells of ‌the cowherd women ​who loved Krishna ​past shame, past ​reason — their ‌love the tradition’s highest ​image of devotion: ​uncalculating, unrequited-looking, and ​finally rewarded. The ‌rasa-theologians read it ​as the soul’s ​love for god; ​the devotees simply ‌wept.

### The Chant ​Goes Global (Modern ‌Kīrtana)

From Caitanya’s ​sixteenth-century Bengali kīrtans ‌to the Hare ​Krishna movement’s twentieth-century ‌global sankīrtana, the ‌name-chant carried bhakti ​around the world. ​The mahāmantra — ​sixteen words, one ​call — became ‌the most widely ‌sung Sanskrit formula ​on earth.
